content:
According to reports yesterday, Apple has agreed to comply with "more equitable" app tracking transparency rules in the European Union, following an investigation by German antitrust regulators.

Apple said it is doing so voluntarily, and as far as we understand, it will make a total of eight changes to comply with the regulations...

Developers typically collect far more personal data than is necessary for an app's functionality. One example cited by Apple is so-called app tracking, which uses the interests inferred from the apps you install to serve you personalised ads, whether within apps or on the web. App Tracking Transparency (ATT) gives you a choice over whether this data can be collected and used in this way.

Apple said yesterday that the Federal Cartel Office (FCO) acknowledged the value of giving users a choice; indeed, the FCO's report said they welcomed ATT from a data protection perspective, as did other German privacy regulators.

The FCO's objection appears to be that Apple's existing prompts make app tracking sound scarier than it actually is. The iPhone maker will make eight changes to address this — including removing the word "tracking".

  • Change the colour of the icon element at the top of the prompt from orange to blue
  • Update the ATT prompt to display full-page
  • Remove the word "tracking" from both the ATT prompt and the personalised ads prompt
  • Change the choice buttons for ATT from "Allow" and "Ask App Not to Track" to "Allow" and "Decline"
  • Allow formatting changes (such as bold, italics, and bullet points) to be added to the ATT prompt
  • Add an option for developers to display an additional page of information directly from the prompt, providing further GDPR details. Developers can already do this with their own prompts prior to the ATT prompt.
  • Allow developers to re-display the ATT prompt one year after a user makes a decision, regardless of whether the choice at that time was "Allow" or "Decline"
  • Make minor wording adjustments to the personalised ads prompt to make it clearer, though without any change to the effect or meaning of the language in question

Apple told us they are committed to ensuring ATT continues to be available in EU countries, and that the move is welcomed by privacy advocacy groups, data protection authorities, and iPhone users.

The company reiterated that its own apps do not display the ATT prompt because they do not use personal data collected from apps to deliver targeted advertising or measure advertising effectiveness. They emphasised that third-party apps are treated exactly the same way — if they don't collect this data, they don't need to display the prompt.

9to5Mac's Take

This appears to be the best outcome for everyone involved. iPhone users will continue to make a choice, but the prompt will more accurately reflect the decision they are being asked to make — choosing between personalised ads and no personalised ads.

The investigation also addressed outside concerns about Apple's own advertising sales business. The company has made clear that it does not use its own apps to collect data for personalised advertising, nor to measure advertising effectiveness.
